name: Shave your head
lead: Shaving the head, or clipping it to a very short uniform length, is a style approach discussed in looksmaxxing communities mainly as a response to thinning or receding hair. Instead of concealing or treating the loss, a person removes the remaining hair so the head reads as one clean, deliberate shape, which proponents say improves how the hairline, skull and face come across.[1][2][3]

Head shaving has a long history across cultures, with records from ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome, and it carries varied meanings including religious practice, military uniformity, punishment, sport, solidarity with cancer patients and fashion.[1] Encyclopedic sources note that buzz cuts can make the face look more defined and are considered suitable for thinning or receding hairlines.[3] For men with pattern hair loss, shaving the head is listed as one way to improve the appearance of the condition, alongside a proposed social theory that fully bald men may signal dominance or high status.[2]
Surveys on how bald men are rated differ between studies and cultures.[2] No clinical studies specifically testing head shaving as an appearance strategy were identified.

angle.text: A shaved or buzzed head removes the contrast between thick and thin areas, so recession and thinning are less visible. Followers say it puts attention on the face and jaw and reads as a deliberate style.

paras: The practice ranges from clipping hair to a very short uniform length to shaving the scalp smooth with a razor or foil shaver. In appearance discussions it is often paired with the idea of embracing baldness, as opposed to treatments, hairpieces or comb-over styles.[2]

The buzz cut family includes the butch cut, with the top clipped to one short length, along with crew cut, flattop and brush cut variations, and fades in which the back and sides are tapered; fade lengths correspond to different clipper guard sizes.[3]

Records of head shaving date to ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome. Egyptian priests removed body hair, and Romans offered a first shave to the gods.[1] Many Buddhist, Hindu and Hare Krishna practitioners shave their heads, often on entering a religious order.[1]

In ancient Greece and much of Babylon, a shaved head marked enslaved people, and in later periods shaving has been used as a punishment or humiliation, including in prisons and in post-war France.[1] Militaries commonly shave recruits' heads, citing hygiene and uniformity; the Wikipedia article credits manual clippers with making buzz cuts popular in the late nineteenth century.[1][3]

Yul Brynner is credited with popularising the look in the 1950s, and shaved heads have been adopted by several subcultures.[1] Shaving by people with hair loss conditions such as alopecia areata has become more socially accepted since the 1990s, and some people shave before or during chemotherapy.[1]

A shaved head on a man is often described as a sign of authority and virility, though the Wikipedia article marks that claim as needing a citation.[1] One proposed social theory holds that men who shave to complete baldness signal dominance, high status or longevity.[2]

Male pattern hair loss is described as a moderately stressful condition that can reduce body-image satisfaction, although most men are reported to cope.[2] Studies on how others perceive bald men conflict: a 2001 South Korean study found most people rated balding men as less attractive, while a 2002 survey of Welsh women rated bald and gray-haired men as quite desirable.[2] Many of these sources are primary studies rather than reviews.[2]

Within appearance communities, shaving is commonly framed as the alternative to treatment for those who prefer not to use or continue medications, and as a style option when hair loss is advanced. Threads on looksmax.org ask what makes a buzz cut look good and why it suits some men, and members trade clipper guard suggestions, for example a 5 or 6 guard for a short spiky buzz.[4][5]
Reports of how it is received vary by individual head shape, skin and facial features, and no controlled studies were found on these claims.
No studies found. Related published work concerns how observers rate balding men generally, with conflicting results across cultures.[2]

lore.intro: Hair-loss and style threads discuss buzz cuts and full shaves as an answer to thinning, and ask which cuts and guard lengths suit particular faces.[4][5]

claims.claim: Shaving a thinning head looks better than a partially covered scalp
claims.believers: Proponents say a uniform shaved or buzzed head reads as intentional and removes the contrast of thin patches, and that it signals confidence.[4]
claims.experts: Published perception research is mixed: a 2001 Korean study rated balding men as less attractive, whereas a 2002 Welsh survey rated bald men as quite desirable.[2]

claims.claim: Embracing baldness signals dominance or high status
claims.believers: Some commentators say shaved men are perceived as more masculine or authoritative.
claims.experts: The idea is described as a proposed social theory in encyclopedic summaries of male pattern hair loss; it is not established.[2]

claims.claim: A buzz cut makes the face look more defined
claims.believers: Members of looksmax.org threads ask what features a buzz cut flatters, treating the cut as a way to show off skull shape and the jaw.[5]
claims.experts: The Wikipedia article on buzz cuts says the style can make the face look more defined; no controlled studies were found.[3]

card.summary: Clip or shave down to embrace thinning hair; a style choice with mixed perception research and no clinical trials.
card.aka: Buzz cut, bald fade, embracing baldness
card.note: Perception studies on bald men conflict; sun protection for the scalp is commonly advised by dermatology bodies.

quick.overview:
Shaving the head means removing remaining hair to a short uniform length or smooth scalp, often as an alternative to concealing or treating hair loss. It has a long cultural history with religious, military, sporting and fashion meanings.

In appearance communities it is often presented as a clean, confident option for men with receding or thinning hair. Published research on how bald or shaved men are perceived is mixed.
quick.mechanism: Hair is cut with clippers or shaved with a razor. It does not change the underlying hair growth cycle or treat hair loss; it changes how the remaining hair and scalp appear.
quick.risks: Documented risks are minor: razor irritation or nicks and, for exposed scalp, sun exposure. No clinical studies on appearance outcomes were found.
